newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: FOCUS - OPEC seen freezing output quotas.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - OPEC seen freezing output quotas.

text.p: OPEC ministers who meet in Vienna this week are likely to freeze current output quotas and try to curb violations, in hope of protecting oil prices against the possible early resumption of sales by Iraq.

Iraq's ambassador at the United Nations, Nizar Hamdoon, said on Monday that Baghdad had agreed to all U.N. conditions that had held up implementing an oil-for-food accord designed to ease the 1991 Gulf War embargo on Iraqi oil exports.

Benchmark light crude oil prices, lately on a strong rally, initially fell almost 40 cents to $22.66 per barrel on the news from New York, although a Security Council sanctions committee has yet to approve a pricing formula that would actually trigger the resumed flow of Iraqi oil.

The Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) which begins a scheduled twice-yearly conference on Wednesday had already pencilled a return of Iraqi oil to its production quota system when it last met, in June.

Its problem is that several of the 11 cartel members are cheating on their assigned supply quotas, and total OPEC daily volume is already almost a million barrels above the intended ceiling of 25.03 million - even before Iraqi exports flow.
"We have to do something", said Libyan minister Abdullah al-Badri, admitting the quota violations and urging action. He said of the Iraq news that "we will find a way out".
Another early arrival in Vienna for Wednesday's talks, Nigerian minister Dan Etete, predicted no change on current quotas. "We will keep the quotas. I don't think anyone wants a change," he said.
Hamdoon said in New York that Iraqi oil could flow in December. The U.N. deal would permit sales worth $2 billion over six months to buy food and medicine. But it has repeatedly been held up.

OPEC's solace, if it really now is going to take effect, is that prices are riding high at the moment. An average of almost $20 per barrel so far this year is up $3 from 1995 and is the firmest since the Gulf War.
The higher prices added up to a windfall extra $30 billion in revenues for the OPEC exporters whose economies were crimped in recent years when oil languished in the bargain basement.
Saudi Arabia, for instance, which produces a third of all cartel oil, can expect $10 billion of excess to deal with a projected 1996 deficit of almost $5 billion.

"It's cold but I hope it gets colder", OPEC secretary-general Rilwanu Lukman of Nigeria told lobby reporters, observing that an early winter in the United States and Europe is firing up demand for fuel.
New supply from non-OPEC exporters also has not built up as fast as oil firms, who were content to operate with low stocks, had predicted this year.
Traders said that the cold weather and the lag in non-OPEC output may limit the decline in prices on the Iraqi news.
"The market is bound to fall on this type of news but it is still focussed on winter and heating oil demand," said Alistair Harris of brokers Mees Pierson Derivatives in London.

The benchmark Brent Blend crude oil dropped in London by almost 40 cents when Hamdoon's comments were first reported but then rebounded and were soon only some 25 cents weaker, trading just below $23 per barrel (42 US gallons).
